Going Off to New York c
In 1987's The Secret of My Success, Michael J. Fox plays a kid
from Kansas who comes to New York to conquer the business
world and discovers there's no such thing as an overnight
success. But just give him a week or two...
The Secret of My Success was the 20th feature film of director
Herbert Ross, whose credits include such diverse motion
pictures as Play It Again, Sam, The Sunshine Boys, Footloose,
My Blue Heaven, Steel Magnolias and The Turning Point (for
which Ross won an Oscar® nomination and a Golden Globe).
Ross described The Secret of My Success as "a comedy of
manners, complete with crisscrossing romantic interests and
mistaken identities." In addition to an affinity for this type of
comedy, Ross was drawn to The Secret of My Success
because, he says, it takes place in New York, "the ultimate
metropolis on the threshold of the nineties."
HERBERT ROSS: I made a choice early on to present a very
stylized view of New York. It's New York as perceived by
Brantley [Michael J. Fox] as the epitome of all that is
wonderful about technology, all that is beautiful about
architecture, all that is fascinating about the incredible
diversity of races and people who live in America. So I
think this film says quite a lot, albeit
in a comic way, about how we see, how we think and
how we feel about the world we live in in the late 1980s.
As crucial as the city of New York was to the theme of the
film, Michael J. Fox is to the tone. Ross wanted to take full
advantage of the young star's talent in developing the story
of a renegade employee who gets to the top by unorthodox
means. "Once I knew that he was going to play the role,"
said the director, "it clarified for me the way the rest of
MICHAEL J. FOX: I like to make people laugh, and whether I
play a dramatic or comedic role, I also try to make people see
something of themselves in what I'm doing. In Brantley, I hope
everyone will see a bit of the hustler in themselves, and
I hope they will also see his self-deprecating sense of humor.
Starring opposite Fox as Christy, an aristocratic junior
executive, is Helen Slater, of whom Ross said, "Besides being
a very beautiful girl, Helen has those wonderful qualities of
breeding that Grace Kelly brought to her roles. This is
important because in the beginning Christy is the mistress
of an older man, and she has to carry herself with class."
Researching her role, Slater spent time watching career women
at New York's City Hall.iThe women seem curt, almost robotic
in a sense, wanting to succeed and not wanting to be looked
at as women first," Slater observed. "So my first instinct was
for Christy to look very military and dress in blue suits.
But Herb wanted to make her softer and bring out more
of her feminine qualities, which turned out to be the best
choice because it adds a little more grit that she's willing to
be both a woman and an executive."
Rounding out the featured cast are two accomplished actors
who honed their skills on stage, screen and TV. the late
Richard Jordan as philandering chief executive Howard Prescott
and Margaret Whitton as Vera, the neurotically erotic corporate
wife who seduces Brantley. In creating a history for her
character, Whitton felt that Vera had been the daughter of a
wealthy industrialist who created the corporation. "I think she
probably took a look at Howard Prescott [Jordan] when he was
young and ambitious, fell madly in love and helped him attain
his position. As the years went on, he began to neglect her,
The Secret of My Success gave Italian cinematographer
Carlo di Palma the opportunity to capture the dynamic,
cosmopolitan atmosphere of New York on several levels.
The shots were designed as a pictorial presentation of the
main characters' dreams and ambitions. Di Palma began
his career in his native Italy, where his early films
The production company set up camera positions in 35
locations across the city, carefully avoiding rush hour when
shooting at busy commuter crossroads such as the Port
Authority Bus Terminal or the Staten Island Ferry. Principal
office sequences were filmed at the headquarters of the
International Paper Company, on the 43rd and 44th floors
of the building just south of Rockefeller Center, where
virtually every window provided a spectacular view.
Another large-scale filming site was a 300-acre estate
overlooking the Hudson River near Mount Kisco, one hour
from midtown Manhattan. The property, which was built in the
mid-1920s and modeled after Thomas Jefferson's Monticello,
had recently been bequeathed to the State of New York by
the Lasdon family. Additional interior scenes were filmed at
In The Secret of My Success, much of the narrative is
conveyed by musical montage. This presented a unique
challenge to Grammy Award-winning artist David Foster,
who composed the score. "I knew we were going to have
several big sequences in which music would be absolutely
essential to achieving the overall effect," director Ross
noted. "So I wanted to have the best musician available,
and David is one of the best."
The Secret of My Success reunited Ross with Academy
Award™-winning editor Paul Hirsch. Their other films
together included Footloose and Steel Magnolias.
"This film celebrates equal opportunity," Ross summarized,
"and the idea that anybody given the pluck, intelligence, skills
and willfulness can climb their way to the top, succeed in
business, make their fortune, get the girl of their dreams
and achieve all the things that the best of technology
and culture have to offer us."

titleInMenusEvidence: HUDSON HAWK / The- / Whole / Nine Yards
discs.note: Box-set disc. The label WILLIS is the ACTOR, not a title, and is shared with vol-willis-8310784000 (a different film). The menus name three Bruce Willis films -- SUNSET, HUDSON HAWK and 'The Whole Nine Yards' (OCR splits it across three observations: 'The-' / 'Whole' / 'Nine Yards') -- and only the last is this disc's feature. Label -> film is not 1:1 here.

Box-set disc, same WILLIS label as vol-willis-7867269120 but a different film. The menus name 'Jackal' (without the leading 'The'), MERCURY RISING and ALPHA DOG. Only 5 OCR lines on the whole disc; nothing marks which of the three names is the feature.
